arguments.content:
# 01_cover

Good morning. Today we're diving into the 2024 Stack Overflow Developer Survey — the largest and most comprehensive developer survey in the world.

This year's edition captured responses from over 65,000 developers across more than 180 countries, giving us a robust dataset to benchmark compensation, employment patterns, and workplace preferences. [Pause]

Our goal: equip you with actionable data points to calibrate your hiring and retention strategies for the coming year.

Key points: (1) Survey scale provides statistical confidence (2) Global reach enables regional comparisons (3) Focus on actionable benchmarks
Duration: 1 minute

---

# 02_employment_status

[Transition] Let's start with the employment landscape — who's working, and how.

Globally, 84% of respondents are currently employed, with full-time roles at 69%. But here's what should get your attention: in the U.S., full-time employment dropped from 69% to 64.8% year-over-year. [Data] That's roughly a four-percentage-point decline — significant in a single year. [Pause]

Meanwhile, freelancing and contracting remain strong at 16.4%, suggesting the gig economy continues to pull talent away from traditional employment. Regional patterns vary: the UK and Ukraine skew toward contracting, while Germany and India show more students entering the pipeline.

Key points: (1) U.S. full-time employment declining (2) Freelancing holding steady at 16%+ (3) Regional differences in non-FT employment
Duration: 2 minutes

---

# 03_work_environment

[Transition] Now let's look at where developers are actually working — remote, hybrid, or in-person.

The headline: hybrid remains king at 42%, unchanged from 2023. But the real story is the steady climb of in-person work — from 15% in 2022 to 20% in 2024. [Data] That's a 33% increase in office attendance over just two years. [Pause]

Remote work has correspondingly declined from about 43% to 38%. The implication for your workforce planning is clear: return-to-office mandates are gaining traction industry-wide, but forcing the issue risks losing talent to the 42% of organizations still offering hybrid arrangements.

Key points: (1) Hybrid dominates at 42% (2) In-person rising steadily (3) Remote declining but still substantial
Duration: 2 minutes

---

# 04_salary_by_role

[Transition] With employment context established, let's get to what everyone wants to know — compensation.

This chart ranks median annual salary by developer type from our 22,677 salary responses. Senior Executives lead at $127,000, followed closely by Developer Advocates at $124,000 — a role that barely existed a decade ago. [Pause]

[Data] Notice the gap: leadership and DevRel roles all clear $110K, while the most common hands-on roles — full-stack at $63K and front-end at $49K — sit significantly lower. SRE and Cloud Infrastructure Engineers, at $99K and $97K respectively, represent the highest-paid purely technical roles.

Key points: (1) Leadership roles command $115K+ (2) SRE/Cloud are top technical salaries (3) Common roles like full-stack sit at $63K
Duration: 2 minutes

---

# 05_experience_vs_salary

[Transition] Salary alone doesn't tell the full story — experience matters. Let's see how they interact.

This scatter plot maps each developer type by average years of experience against median salary. The upper-right cluster tells a clear story: Senior Executives, Dev Advocates, and Managers all have 15+ years of experience and six-figure salaries. [Pause]

But look at the outliers. SRE engineers earn $99K with just 10 years average experience — punching well above their experience weight class. Conversely, Product Managers at 14 years average experience earn only $80K. [Data] Students at the bottom left — $15K with 2 years — serve as a baseline reference.

Key points: (1) Experience-salary correlation is strong but not linear (2) SRE overperforms on experience-to-pay ratio (3) Leadership cluster in upper-right
Duration: 2 minutes

---

# 06_salary_by_language

[Transition] Now let's shift from roles to tools — specifically, how programming language choice correlates with pay.

The pattern is striking: niche functional languages dominate the top. Erlang developers earn $97K median, Clojure $95K, and Elixir $93K — all with roughly 11-12 years of experience. [Pause]

[Data] Compare that to mainstream languages: JavaScript at $64K, PHP at $49K — despite similar or higher average experience. The overall salary range has also compressed, dropping roughly $10K compared to 2023.

The takeaway for hiring: if you're trying to attract Erlang or Clojure talent, you're competing in a $90K+ market. If you're staffing JavaScript roles, the market is more accessible at $64K.

Key points: (1) Functional language devs earn 40%+ premium (2) Overall salary range compressed vs. 2023 (3) Language choice is a salary proxy
Duration: 2 minutes

---

# 07_company_size_purchasing

[Transition] Let's zoom out from individual compensation to the organizational context — company size and purchasing power.

Nearly half of all developers — 47% — work at organizations with fewer than 100 employees. The largest segment is 20-99 employees at 21%. This has direct implications for how you source talent and how vendors should approach the market. [Pause]

On the purchasing side, 62% of developers report having influence over technology decisions at their organizations. [Data] That's nearly two-thirds. Senior executives have near-universal influence at 99%, but engineering managers at 87% and product managers at 77% are also key decision-makers.

How do developers evaluate? [Data] 75% start with a free trial, 73% ask other developers. The peer recommendation channel is almost as powerful as hands-on experience.

Key points: (1) 47% at sub-100 orgs (2) 62% influence purchases (3) Free trials and peer recommendations drive adoption
Duration: 2 minutes

---

# 08_key_takeaways

[Transition] Let me close with five actionable takeaways from everything we've covered.

First, full-time employment is softening — build contractor capacity into your workforce plans. Second, in-person mandates are growing, but hybrid still dominates — force return-to-office at your own risk. [Pause]

Third, DevRel, SRE, and leadership roles command premium pay — budget accordingly or risk losing these critical roles. Fourth, language specialization correlates strongly with compensation — niche functional language talent costs 40% more than mainstream. [Pause]

And fifth — perhaps the most actionable insight for those on the vendor side — developers are the key purchase influencers. [Data] With 62% having a say, your go-to-market strategy should engage individual contributors directly through free trials and developer communities, not just management.

Key points: (1) Plan for contractor mix (2) Hybrid is table stakes (3) Premium roles need premium budgets (4) Language = salary proxy (5) Engage ICs directly
Duration: 2 minutes
